title: 30 PGPR, drought, and nitrogen effects in Schedonorus arundinaceus on yield, CP, ADF, aNDF, and Lignin
content:
Abstract
Schedonorus arundinaceus, commonly known as tall fescue, plays a vital role in livestock production systems, especially in the southern United States. This cool-season C3 grass is extensively used for grazing, hay production, and stockpiling, providing a reliable forage source for cattle and other ruminants. Tall fescue is particularly valued for its adaptability to a range of environmental conditions, notably its drought tolerance and capacity to grow under low fertility soils. The KY31 variety, in particular, exhibits enhanced drought resistance due to its symbiotic relationship with the fungal endophyte Epichloe coenophiala, which also contributes to the grass’s overall hardiness. However, despite these advantages, rising nitrogen (N) fertilizer costs and the increasing frequency of drought events present significant challenges for maintaining forage yield and quality, necessitating alternative management strategies. The greenhouse study conducted at the Plant Science Research Center at Auburn University aimed to evaluate the combined effects of plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) inoculation, different levels of N fertilization, and drought stress on the yield and forage quality of two tall fescue varieties, KY31 and KY32. The experimental design consisted of four PGPR treatments (no PGPR, Corteva Utrisha-N, DH267, and DH44), three N levels (100%, 50%, and 25% of the recommended rate), and two water treatments (well-watered and drought conditions). Forage quality parameters assessed included crude protein (CP), acid detergent fiber (ADF), neutral detergent fiber (aNDF), and lignin. The results indicated significant effects of variety (P<.001), N rate (P<.0001), and water treatment (P<.0001) on yield, with KY31 generally outperforming KY32. As expected, drought conditions led to a reduction in yield across all treatments. PGPR inoculation, however, did not significantly impact overall yield (P=0.627). CP showed a significant four-way interaction effect between variety, PGPR, N rate, and water treatment (P=0.029), likely due to a concentration effect from reduced plant growth. ADF and aNDF both showed a three-way interaction between variety, PGPR, and N rate with P-values of (P=0.049) and (P=0.045) respectively. Additionally, KY32 inoculated with the DH267 strain showed an increase in ADF, while the DH44 inoculation at 25% N level resulted in decreased ADF. These findings suggest that PGPR may influence forage quality through complex interactions involving variety, PGPR, N availability, and water status in some parameters, these can potentially be used in developing sustainable pasture management practices. Further research into optimizing these interactions could provide valuable insights for improving forage production and quality in livestock systems facing economic and environmental pressures.
